title: Your chats on every device — round 8: the last four choices

steps.intro: Measured on your desktop: a chat is its lines, plus a small folder beside it. The lines already hold every helper's task and its final report. The folder holds each helper's step-by-step working file (1 to 2 MB each), long outputs the assistant saved to reread, and the chat's plan and to-do list. Separately, the assistant has a setup that belongs to the device, not to any chat: skills, plugins, connected tools and your global instructions.

steps.path: A chat continued on a second device
steps.headline: How much of a chat's folder should travel with it?
steps.today: Only the chat's lines sync. Helper working files, saved outputs, the plan and the to-do list stay on the device that made them. Helper files are 8.4 GB on your desktop, half of everything stored.
steps.problem: A chat continued elsewhere without its folder still has every helper's final report, but the assistant cannot send a helper a follow-up, cannot reread a saved output, and loses the plan it was following. You called that lost work.
steps.proposal: Under every option, the rule for what belongs to a chat is by location: whatever sits in that chat's own folder. Documents inside a project travel as project files, already decided. Pasted images and undo history are dropped, as you said was fine.

options.label: Recent chats complete everywhere; older chats fetch their folder when opened
pros: A chat used in the last 48 hours is whole on every device, so switching devices mid-work loses nothing.
A phone holds megabytes, not 8.4 GB.
Matches the relay's 48 hours, so there is one time rule to remember.
cons: Opening an older chat on another device waits a moment while its folder arrives.
If the only device holding an old chat's folder is off, you can continue with the helpers' reports only. The notice says so before you continue.

options.label: Every chat's folder on every device, always
pros: Nothing is ever fetched late; every chat is whole everywhere, even offline.
cons: Every device, phones included, stores the full 8.4 GB and growing.
A new device's first sync takes far longer.

options.label: Lines only; the folder stays where it was made
cons: The lost work you described: no helper follow-ups, no saved outputs, no plan after a switch.

steps.path: A chat continued on a device with a different setup
steps.headline: Should keeping skills, plugins and connected tools the same on every device be part of this work?
steps.today: The setup is copied to a cloud backup once a day and never brought back down. Each device has whatever you installed on it.
steps.problem: A chat that used a skill on the desktop moves to a phone without it. The assistant there cannot use that skill, and may behave differently because your global instructions differ too.
steps.proposal: Under every option, the Continue here notice names what this device lacks, as you already decided.

options.label: A separate card, built after chats sync
pros: Chats on every device arrives sooner and with less risk.
The setup has hard cases of its own that deserve their own questions: a plugin that cannot run on a phone, and sign-ins for connected tools, which should not be copied around lightly.
cons: Until that card is built you install skills on each device yourself, and a moved chat can be missing some.

options.label: Part of this design
pros: The full promise from day one: every device behaves the same.
cons: Roughly doubles the size of this work, and adds several more rounds of questions before anything is built.

options.label: Leave setups separate for good
pros: Each device stays exactly as you set it up; nothing installs itself.
cons: A moved chat keeps hitting missing skills forever.

steps.intro: Two older ideas overlap with the new system. Each question asks whether it stays.

steps.path: Settings, Remote access; and the phone's Connect to a computer screen
steps.headline: What should happen to today's remote access?
steps.today: The phone app or a web browser can open one computer's whole YouCoded: its chats, its settings, its files, everything on that computer's screen. It works only through Tailscale, and one computer at a time.
steps.problem: The new system gives every device every chat without Tailscale. Keeping both means two ways to reach a chat from the phone, with different rules and different screens.

options.label: Replace it inside the apps; keep the open-in-a-browser view
pros: One way to reach chats in the apps, with no Tailscale and no Connect screen.
A browser on a borrowed computer can still open one of your devices, and that is also how you look inside a super-host.
Less old code to keep working.
cons: The phone app shows its own settings and files plus all your chats, no longer the computer's whole screen. Changing a setting on the desktop from the phone would need the browser view.
The browser view still needs Tailscale, as today.

options.label: Keep remote access as it is, beside the new system
pros: Nothing you use today goes away.
cons: Two ways to do nearly the same thing; users must learn which is which.
Both must be kept working and secure.

options.label: Replace it everywhere, the browser view too
pros: Simplest: one system and nothing else.
cons: No way to use YouCoded from a device without the app installed.
A super-host would have no screen to look at.

steps.path: Backup & Sync in settings, the relay choice
steps.headline: Should users be able to run a relay of their own that is not a super-host?
steps.today: Neither exists yet. You approved the super-host: one of your own devices at home, always on, holding everything, able to read your chats because it is yours. Our relay holds locked lines it cannot read.
steps.problem: A self-run relay would be a third thing: a copy of our relay on the user's own account or machine, blind like ours. It adds a setting and an install path, for a job the super-host already does.
steps.proposal: Under both options, using no keeper at all still works: your devices catch each other up whenever two are on together.

options.label: No. Self-hosting means running a super-host
pros: One thing to explain and one thing to set up.
Fewer settings: use the YouCoded relay, or your super-host, or neither.
cons: A user with no always-on device at home, who also does not want our relay, has no middle option.
Nobody can run a blind relay for family or friends; a super-host can read what it holds, so it only suits its owner.

options.label: Yes. Offer it as a third choice
pros: Covers users who want nothing of ours and have no home device to leave on.
One person could run a blind relay for several people.
cons: A third thing to build, test and explain, used by very few.
Setting it up is technical: an account with a hosting company and a guided install.
